A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Firewalls to Secure Dynamic LLM Agentic Networks. Their text, figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: v3 reports original GPT-4o simulations measuring privacy leakage, malicious actions, upselling, and benign adaptability in Section 6, with conversation examples in the appendices.

after.justification: v6 reports original firewall evaluations, component ablations, and held-out-persona results in Section 5 and the appendices. The unprotected baselines are explicitly imported from ConVerse, but the firewall results qualify as original empirical work.

M1.justification: The three-firewall framework becomes a dual-firewall architecture: trajectory self-correction is removed, while input conversion gains learned closed schemas, deterministic validation, and reversible string anonymization. Data abstraction receives raw data and domain rules only, whereas v3 also supplied the user goal (v3 Table 49; v6 Algorithm 5).

E1.justification: Travel planning is retained, while evaluation expands to real-estate search and insurance through ConVerse, with distinct service databases and contextual disclosure requirements. v6 also covers broader privacy targets and security scenarios, including unauthorized email sending, beyond v3's travel-focused experiments.

E2.justification: v3 compares baseline and task-confined assistants alongside incremental data-plus-trajectory and three-firewall configurations. v6 removes the separately evaluated task-confined and trajectory-based comparators, using no-firewall, data-only, and language-only configurations against the dual firewall (Tables 6–7). This substantially changes the evaluated comparison set.

E3.justification: GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash replace the single GPT-4o setting; Pro appears only in travel results. v6 uses GPT-5 judging against benchmark annotations and overall plan ratings/coverage instead of many earlier item-level counts. Rule generation changes to Claude Sonnet 4 with two personas per domain and explicit held-out-persona evaluation.

E4.justification: v3's incremental firewall and rule-refinement comparisons are replaced by separate data-only, language-only, joint, and unprotected ablations for privacy and security. v6 separately quantifies rule-generating versus held-out personas, extending v3's generalization evidence. Earlier benign-offer adaptability analyses and complete benign traces disappear, while new cross-domain attack case studies appear.

E5.justification: v3 reports averages from ten runs per condition without confidence intervals. v6 introduces systematic 95% Wilson score intervals for attack success and t-distribution intervals for utility metrics (Section 5.3). This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, without establishing that repeated-run counts increased.

E6.justification: v3 reports medical leakage falling from 70% to 0% and calendar-deletion success from 45% to 0% (Tables 3–4). v6 replaces these evaluations with new ConVerse results, including aggregate GPT-5 privacy ASR of 84.68% versus 10.20% and security ASR of 60.39% versus 3.42% (Tables 12–13), plus new utility and ablation results. These are different experimental settings, not direct improvements over v3's scores.

T1.justification: v6 adds the structured-language definition L=(K,V,T) and explicit closed-vocabulary, type-validation, and string-isolation properties in Section 4.1. v3 discussed a closed language as future work. This adds limited formal specification and reasoning; neither version develops substantial theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 centers contributions on agent requirements, a new travel testbed, and practical layered mitigation. v6 centers learned dual-firewall context projections and claims structural exclusion of free-form manipulation regardless of attack sophistication. The original testbed contribution is replaced by evaluation on the separately cited ConVerse benchmark.

C2.justification: v6 adds explanations of component complementarity, possible conservative-judge contributions to residual privacy failures, and generalization through domain norms. It explicitly excludes poisoned knowledge bases and discusses compositional privacy and computational overhead, while dropping v3's warning about abstraction limiting complex reasoning. Its utility-preservation interpretation is broader than the coverage declines reported in Tables 4–5 and 12.

D1.justification: v6 adds verifier and anonymization pseudocode, schema constraints, rule-generation sampling details, and generated-rule statistics. Conversely, v3's extensive simulator, assistant, attacker, and judge prompts, synthetic-profile listings, and travel-option inventory are no longer supplied in full. The code link also points to a different repository.

R1.justification: v6 substantially expands positioning around classical contextual integrity, pre-LLM multi-agent privacy, newer structural security defenses, and contextual-reasoning methods. Additions include Barth et al., Such et al., Costa et al., Lan et al., Yi et al., and ConVerse. Much of v3's travel-planning literature discussion is removed, and benchmark construction is repositioned as prior work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around two trust boundaries and context projection. The earlier testbed-centered narrative and eleven-part appendix organization become a method-centered account with four appendices. This is substantial restructuring beyond terminology changes.

P2.justification: The two-column conference layout becomes a single-column manuscript. The earlier schematics are replaced by redesigned dual-firewall diagrams, results use new model-by-firewall table structures with confidence intervals, and five algorithm blocks are added. Extensive prompt tables and long conversation displays give way to shorter specifications and revised qualitative comparisons.

improvement.justification: v6 implements the closed-language protection left as future work in v3 and materially strengthens validation through multiple models, additional domains, component ablations, and uncertainty reporting. These gains outweigh the loss of full prompt appendices. However, its broad utility and security summaries need qualification: Table 12 shows GPT-5 coverage decreasing from 96.55% to 91.49%, and Table 13 reports Claude Sonnet 4 security ASR of 4.19%, exceeding the claimed under-4% level.
